scripts.opening:opening:
[ominous] JAUNT: THE LAST PULLMAN TWIN. Dusk on a Monday in November 1904. The lamps are coming on along Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] Four stops, from the biggest house on the street to the house of the one Pullman child who turned out the way her father wanted. George Pullman built sleeping cars, a company town and a fortune. [short pause] [darkly] He could not build sons. His twins, George Jr. and Sanger, were born in 1875 into more money than almost anyone in America, [wryly] and spent their lives showing the city what that does to a boy.

[short pause] [quietly] Start at the Pullman house, where the widow lives with the shades half drawn.
scripts.stop:widow: [measured] 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house, the biggest pile on the block. Harriett Sanger married George Pullman in 1867, and they had four children: Florence, Harriett, and in 1875 the twins, George Jr. and Walter Sanger, whom everyone calls Sanger. George Pullman died in 1897 and left his widow this house, which she still keeps. [short pause] [darkly] To the twins he left a judgment, written into his will: "Pullman's will stipulated that the twins were to be given a yearly stipend of only $3,000." [short pause] [wryly] Their father knew them. Mrs. Pullman's carriage is at the door; Henry Windish, the coachman, has it ready, and Miss Robinson, her companion, is with her. [short pause] The house will be razed in 1922. Go round to the glasshouse, where the boys grew up.
scripts.stop:boys: [amused] The Pullman conservatory, glass and palms at the side of the house. The twins grew up here. They were schooled at home on Prairie Avenue, [conspiratorially] and the story went round that they were "arranging and promoting pit bull fights". [laughs] As teenagers they "frequently were seen riding around Chicago in cabs filled with champagne bottles." Their father sent them east to a training school for Harvard, where "Sanger and George were ranked 147 and 148 out of a class of 148 students." [short pause] [chuckles] Last and next to last, side by side, as close as twins should be. [short pause] [thoughtful] And the cleverer twin was Sanger: "widely acknowledged as the smarter of the 2". [short pause] [sadly] It never helped him. Cross the street to look at the house where the other twin's story ended.
scripts.stop:george: [quietly] From the west side of the street, look back at the Pullman house in the dusk. [short pause] The other twin is gone. George Jr. secretly married Lynn Fernald, "his brother's betrothed": [incredulous] he stole his own twin's bride. A man named Frederick Bowers sued him for $100,000, "eventually settling for $50,000." [short pause] [softly] Then in November 1901 George died of pneumonia, at 26. The World printed a headline: "Death of George Pullman a Warning to Rich Fathers." [long pause] So Sanger is the last of the twins. He is 29 now, and still poor with money: thrown out of the New York Athletic Club for unpaid dues, and his debts so tangled that a creditor once held his sister-in-law's luggage for five months. [short pause] [sighs] His mother has paid before. Walk south to the sister who never needed paying for.
scripts.stop:sister: [warmly] 1912 Prairie, the Lowden house. Florence, the eldest Pullman child, married Frank Orren Lowden, a lawyer, and here they live with their children. Lowden is a lawyer, and when trouble comes to the family, it tends to come to his office. [short pause] [lowering voice] Their mother once "paid the unnamed woman $10,000 to leave Sanger and never return." [short pause] [tenderly] The children play at their nurse's feet on a quiet Monday evening, the way the twins once did on this same street. [short pause] The house will be razed in 1939. [long pause] [ominous] And the last twin is still out there, riding hard.
scripts.ending:ride: [softly] End of the walk. Sanger Pullman lived nine more months. [short pause] In August 1905 he "died after being thrown from a horse and carriage after yet another wild ride". [long pause] [sadly] His mother had now buried her husband and both her sons; her husband lay in Graceland under a "lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete", so that nobody could ever get at him. [short pause] Nobody could get at the boys, either, not their father, not their money, not their mother's $10,000. [short pause] [darkly] The World had said it in 1901, and it was still true: "a Warning to Rich Fathers."
